report:
**Conclusion: broadly yes, but the benefit is modest and not certain for every product or person.** In women with recurrent *uncomplicated*, symptomatic, culture-confirmed cystitis/UTI, cranberry products (juice, tablets, or capsules) reduce recurrences versus placebo/no treatment in the best current pooled evidence.

The 2023 Cochrane review included 50 randomized studies (8,857 participants) and concluded that cranberry products reduce symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs in women with recurrent UTIs. The proposed mechanism is cranberry proanthocyanidins reducing bacterial attachment to the bladder lining. The effect estimate in this subgroup was about a **26% relative reduction** in recurrence—not complete prevention. Evidence does **not** establish that juice is superior to standardized extracts/capsules, or what exact dose/product formulation works best; studies used varied products and doses.  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD001321.pub6/full  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37068952/

Why the qualified answer? Earlier trials and reviews were inconsistent; an earlier Cochrane update found that adding newer studies made cranberry juice appear less effective than previously thought. This likely reflects variable cranberry active-compound content, adherence (particularly with juice), outcome definitions, and small trials.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23076891/

Thus, cranberry is a reasonable low-risk **non-antibiotic option** for many women with recurrent uncomplicated cystitis, especially if they prefer to avoid prophylactic antibiotics, but it should not replace evaluation of recurrent symptoms or treatment of an acute infection. The AUA guideline specifically addresses this population—women with localized recurrent cystitis—and supports shared decision-making about prevention choices.  
https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/recurrent-uti
